paper_title: Real In, Real Out: What If We Only Use Real Data for Scene Text Editing?

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Aiming to modify textual content while preserving the original style, Scene Text Editing (STE) has significant practical value in many applications. STE typically requires paired images before and after editing for training. However, recent approaches rely heavily on synthetic paired data and complex disentanglement strategies. They struggle to faithfully capture the diversity and complexity of natural scenes, often producing artifacts or hallucinations. In this work, we challenge the common practice and investigate whether STE can be driven by turning each real sample into its own paired supervision. Concretely, we explore multiple ways to disrupt the original image (e.g., Crop, Shuffle, Mask) to construct self-paired training data, and build a strong baseline (TextRIRO}) upon a conditional diffusion architecture. Our experiments show that combining character-column shuffling with image cropping (Shuffle&Crop) effectively destroys text semantics while preserving key style cues, enabling the model to learn editing behaviors directly from the real text image. With this concise yet real-oriented design, TextRIRO achieves promising performance in both accuracy and visual realism across real-world benchmarks, substantially mitigating the synthetic-to-real domain gap. Furthermore, we leverage TextRIRO to build TextRIRO-3M, a large-scale realistic dataset for long-text recognition by concatenating edited and original images. Experimental results show that training recognition models with TextRIRO-3M significantly improves recognition accuracy, demonstrating that TextRIRO provides highly useful training resources for downstream tasks. Overall, TextRIRO lifts STE to realistic, reliable, and widely applicable new levels. Code is available at https://github.com/YesianRohn/TextRIRO.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Scene Text Editing (STE) aims to extract the style of the given text and replace it with new string, while maintaining both visual realism and style consistency [36]. STE is typically formulated as generative task, and its applications grow with the advancement of generative models. It addresses practical needs such as replacing text in images for artistic creation and also facilitates various downstream scene text tasks. Notably, STE shows significant potential in generating data [39] for scene text recognition (STR) [6, 10, 11, 48], as it can generate samples with the same style but different content from existing images. Corresponding authors. Accepted as conference paper at NeurIPS 2026. Figure 1 data-centric view of Scene Text Editing. The comparison of the previous methods and TextRIRO between the data utilization paradigm (left) and the editing results (right). In (e), we present the artifacts and hallucinations of the wrong editing results in (a) and (b). However, it is hardly possible to get different texts with the same background style in real-world scenarios. To address this, previous methods [20, 29, 36, 38, 43] rely heavily on synthetic data, as shown in Fig. 1(a). On the one hand, two-stage explicit disentanglement methods [29, 36, 38] use rendering tools to synthesize paired images with identical style but different text over background image, followed by foreground-background separation and fusion. But they fail to separate text from the background, resulting in incomplete removal of the source text, as shown in cases (1) and (2) in Fig. 1(e). On the other hand, implicit disentanglement approaches [20, 43] leverage various pre-trained models to extract features for directly generating target images, which is less controllable, resulting in hallucinations such as case (3), with misspelled or missing characters. Recent efforts [9, 22, 26] have explored semi-supervised learning with real data by erasing itself and writing back or paired training using pseudo-labeled data, as illustrated in Fig. 1(b). Nevertheless, synthetic data still remains dominant. As evident from the editing results in Fig. 1(e), this branch of methods easily leads to case (4): even when the target text is generated, it often appears mismatched in style or contains visible artifacts. Furthermore, inpainting-based STE paradigms (Fig. 1(c)) mask the text region and attempt to restore it using surrounding context [2, 4, 15, 39]. However, the lack of sufficient style cues makes it difficult to recover the desired appearance, as shown in Fig. 1(f). We are motivated by an observation that prior work has under-emphasized: the domain gap in STE is primarily data problem, and only secondarily an architecture problem. We therefore ask the simplest possible version of the question: What if we only use real data for scene text editing, with neither synthetic triplets nor expensive paired collection? The core challenge is to extract stable style guidance from the source text image while suppressing the 2 side effect from semantic text content. Our key insight is that scene text style mainly lies in low-level cues such as color, texture, and illumination, while semantic text is high-level sequential structure. Based on this, we explore multiple self-paired real-data schemes that force the model to focus on style rather than semantics. Specifically, we experiment with (i) shuffling and recombining the text region either column-wise or block-wise (Shuffle), (ii) cropping local sub-regions (Crop), and (iii) masking parts of the original image (Mask). Empirically, we find that combining column-wise Shuffle with Crop (Shuffle&Crop) achieves the best performance. To realize the idea, we propose TextRIRO, conditional diffusion model that takes only Real data as Input and produces Realistic Output for scene Text editing. During training, TextRIRO applies Shuffle&Crop to real text image to separate its style and semantics, and then reconstructs the original image. By removing the reliance on synthetic data, it overcomes the bottleneck of high-quality generation during inference. For style features, we process them into multi-scale representations and then inject them into the conditional U-Net using the ControlNet-like process [45] for efficient integration. For text encoding, we use an STR pre-trained encoder [16] to extract character-level features, which improves text understanding and enables robust STE transfer. TextRIRO removes the need for explicit or implicit disentanglement and avoids using the synthetic domain as the main training support. On real benchmarks for STE, it produces more realistic results with markedly reduced synthetic flavor. It also achieves higher accuracy on equal-length editing and variable-length editing tasks. These results show that self-paired training on real data effectively moves STE toward realistic generation. We further ask whether STE can help STR data generation [39, 40, 42]. We find that TextRIRO already outperforms existing STE methods, but the editing accuracy still limits direct use as training data. We then use STE as data expansion by concatenating the original image with its edited counterpart. This preserves style but adds content, which yields high-quality, scene-consistent samples for long-text recognition. Starting from the labeled real dataset U14M-Filter [7, 16], we build 3M-scale dataset, TextRIRO-3M. On Union14M-Benchmark [16], training an STR model on mixed TextRIRO-3M and real data improves overall accuracy by 1.91% over real-only baseline, and improves the Multi-words subset by 3.28%. These gains indicate that current STR training data are not saturated and STE-based synthetic data substantially boost STR. In summary, our main contributions are as follows: We propose TextRIRO, novel STE method that trains solely on real data via self-paired supervision. It performs realistic editing without explicit or implicit disentanglement, and it alleviates artifacts and hallucinations caused by the synthetic-to-real domain gap. TextRIRO achieves more realistic and accurate edits on real benchmarks and attains state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance under the stronger criterion of training with edited data. Built on TextRIRO, we create TextRIRO-3M, large-scale realistic composite dataset for long-text recognition. It significantly improves STR, which validates both the realism and the utility of our edited data and demonstrates that STE effectively benefits STR.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Model Perspective on STE Traditional STE methods evolve from GAN-based models [20, 29, 36, 38] to diffusion models [2, 15, 32, 33, 43, 47] and, more recently, to Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) [9, 44]. Early STE models employ GANs to directly edit foreground text, as seen in SRNet [36] and its multistage framework for reconstructing background, rendering text, and fusing outputs. Later works expand capabilities: SwapText [38] handles curved text, STEFANN [29] focuses on character-level control, and TextStyleBrush [20] leverages StyleGAN2 [19] for self-supervised style-content disentanglement. Diffusion models advance STE further: DiffSTE [15] uses dual encoders, DiffUTE [2] introduces inpainting and OCR-guided encoding, TextDiffuser [3] and UDiffText [47] use segmentation masks for better generation. 3 Figure 2 TextRIRO pipeline. (a) At training time, single real image Itgt is pushed through content-destructive, style-preserving operator to produce pseudo-source Isrc. ViT-based style encoder emits multi-scale features that are injected into the denoising U-Net through ControlNet-style zero-convolutions, while text encoder pre-trained on real scene text with an autoregressive STR objective supplies the target-text conditioning. (b) At inference time, the same U-Net follows the standard SD denoising schedule. (c) Our text encoder is lightweight character tokenizer trained jointly with an STR decoder via next-token prediction. (d) The edited image is validated by an independent STR model and, if : trainable. accepted, concatenated with its original to build style-consistent long-text sample for STR. : frozen, Frameworks like AnyText [33] and AnyText2 [32] unify multilingual editing via ControlNet [45]. TextCtrl [43] disentangles style conditions directly in diffusion models. Meanwhile, DARLING [44] unifies scene text editing, removal, and recognition tasks to leverage these tasks to disentangle task-specific features and RS-STE [9] utilizes scene text recognition to assist scene text editing. These two approaches highlight synergy across scene text tasks. Data Perspective on STE Model advancements in STE are closely tied to the evolution of training data. Early methods use synthetic paired data by rendering tools, e.g., SRNet-Datagen [36]. To include real-world data, RewriteNet [22] uses masked regions and MOSTEL [26] proposes an erasing and writing-back strategy. UMM-based RS-STE [9] adopts reverse self-supervision on real images. In diffusion-based STE, some models (e.g., TextCtrl [43]) disentangle features using synthetic data, while others [3, 33] view STE as masked image inpainting, releasing large real datasets like Anyword-3M [33] and MARIO-10M [3]. However, style consistency can be difficult when context lacks similar references. Benchmarks and datasets for application are also advancing: ScenePair [43] provides high-quality real-world evaluation, and TextSSR [39] generates millions of edited images for STR tasks, demonstrating STEs broader utility.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: The STE process can be formally defined as follows. Denote the input source image as Isrc, the target text as Ttgt, and the editing model as . The objective is to produce the target image Itgt such that: Itgt = Isrc, Ttgt. (1) However, Eq. 1 characterizes the ideal training and inference procedure. In practice, training data rarely provide real triplets Isrc, Ttgt, Itgt. To bridge this gap, Sec. 3.1 introduces self-paired training strategy, Sec. 3.2 presents the unified TextRIRO architecture, and Sec. 3.3 leverages the trained model to expand STR datasets with long-text instances.

sections.title: 3.1 Self-Paired STE Data
sections.content: Most prior data pipelines [26, 36] construct Isrc, Ttgt, Itgt triplets primarily from synthetic text images. The domain gap between synthetic and real scenes limits the ability of STE models and their applications to downstream scene text tasks. Recent methods [9, 26] introduce some real data for unpaired training, yet synthetic samples remain dominant and only partially bridge this gap. Algorithm 1 Self-Paired STE Data Generation Require: Scene text image Itgt, corresponding text label Ttgt, shuffle probability pshuffle Ensure: Generated self-paired source image Isrc 1: Let = Ttgt denote the length of the text label. 2: Partition Itgt along its longest axis into equally sized segments: = {B1, B2, ..., BL}. 3: Sample 0, 1. 4: if < pshuffle then 5: 6: else 7: 8: end if 9: Choose and randomly select consecutive subset of segments from B. 10: Concatenate the selected segments to form Isrc. 11: Return Isrc, Ttgt, Itgt Randomly permute the order of the segments to obtain = {B Set = (i.e., maintain original order). 1, ..., L}. When using an image as Isrc, our goal is to remove its textual content while preserving its style. This motivates simple strategy: scrambling the original image disrupts content while retaining stylistic features. However, since text comprises discrete characters, excessive shuffling fragments glyphs and impairs shape consistency. This presents trade-off: we aim to maximize content removal but minimize stylistic degradation. (1) Text typically aligns along its long axis, and its content and length are known. We exploit this structural prior by dividing the image along its long axis into (L is the number of characters) equal bins. By reordering these bins, we generate the source image Isrc (see Shuffle in Fig. 2), thereby breaking semantic continuity while maintaining local appearance cues. (2) Stripe-based shuffling alone is insufficient for complex text layouts, such as curved or multi-oriented arrangements. To address this, we propose an alternative that reconstructs the image through its sub-patches. The global text arrangement is locally preserved: tilts and curvature manifest within contiguous sub-images. We form Isrc by cropping the original image (as illustrated by Crop in Fig. 2), yielding self-paired data that retain the stylistic integrity of intricate layouts. (3) Combining these two strategies results in more robust and diverse self-paired mechanism. As shown in Fig. 2 (Shuffle then Crop), with probability pshuffle, shuffling is applied before cropping. Otherwise, cropping is applied directly to the original image. Alg. 1 presents the complete algorithm of our self-paired dataset. The subsequent ablation study presents other self-paired methods (e.g., Crop Only, Shuffle Only, Mask) and results, further demonstrating the optimality of the adopted algorithm. 5 Figure 3 Qualitative comparison on ScenePair. Target Reference is the real paired ground truth. Rendering Tool composites the target string on the segmented foreground/background of the source and serves as an accuracy-only reference. TextRIRO is the only method that consistently reproduces the stroke thickness, perspective and illumination of the reference without leaving synthetic residue.

sections.title: 3.2 Model Architecture
sections.content: With the constructed self-paired triplets, TextRIRO maps the perturbed source image Isrc and target text Ttgt into style and text control signals for ControlNet-like diffusion generator [45], as shown in Fig. 2. The style encoder follows TextCtrl [43]: ViT backbone [5] extracts image representations, and lightweight spatial pyramid aggregates them into multi-scale features that are additively injected into the U-Net. For text, we keep character-level encoding [43, 47] but replace synthetic glyph/CLIP pre-training with an autoregressive STR objective on real scene text [16, 30]. This improves real-domain character awareness and aligns recognition with editing. The generator contains VAE for latent mapping, U-Net for denoising, and the above style/text encoders. The VAE and text encoder are frozen, while the style encoder and U-Net are jointly trained with the standard noise-prediction diffusion objective conditioned on style and text. This design is intentionally simple and backbone-agnostic: stronger diffusion backbones or conditioning modules can be substituted when more compute is available. We also evaluate DiT-based conditional control alternative in Tab. 5, where ControlNet-style multi-scale injection remains more effective for fine-grained scene text editing. Detailed feature equations, tokenization, and the training loss are provided in Appendix Sec. 6.1.

sections.title: 3.3 Generating Long-Text Recognition Data
sections.content: After training TextRIRO, we generate style-matched image with the same length but different content for each real input. To ensure correctness, we filter generated samples with an STR model trained on real data and keep only instances whose predicted text matches Ttgt. We then concatenate each filtered image with its original reference to build long-text recognition data, doubling the sequence length. The detailed pipeline and visualizations are illustrated in Fig. 2 (d). This procedure substantially broadens coverage for rare scenarios, such as long and multi-word instances, and it establishes practical connection between STE and STR.

4.2 Ablation Study
Contributions of each core component. Fig. 4 summarizes ablations over the TextRIRO architecture and
self-paired training paradigm. Text encoding is essential: without pre-training, the model fails to learn
reliable character correspondences, while STR pre-training performs better than glyph pre-training because it
is learned directly from real scene text. SD 2.1 provides better VAE reconstruction than SD 1.5, and rectangular
64 × 256 inputs avoid the distortion caused by square resizing. For self-paired data construction, Shuffle&Crop
achieves the best accuracy/realism trade-off. Crop Only lacks diversity, Shuffle Only breaks alignment,
Mask destroys both content and style, Block introduces a strong distribution shift, and removing paired
construction degenerates to identity copying. Fig. 5 visualizes key ablation findings. The Glyph Pre-train
carries strong glyph priors and tends to lose style details, while the STR Pre-train better maintains the original
style during editing. Alternative self-paired constructions also trail Shuffle&Crop in both rendering accuracy
and style fidelity: Shuffle Only and Crop Only give less diversity, and Mask and Block create a large train–test
gap.

sections.title: 4.3 Synthetic Data Utility
sections.content: Despite TextRIROs advances, 10.10% accuracy gap remains compared to training with the same amount of real data. This gap mainly comes from non-trivial number of edit failures that slip into the training set and accumulate errors. TextSSR [39] filters with an STR model to select usable samples, but the retained images largely duplicate styles already present in real data, which causes distribution redundancy and limits data expansion for STR. sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: In this paper, we have introduced TextRIRO, scene text editing method that, for the first time, learns editing purely from real data through self-paired supervision scheme. By disrupting semantic content via targeted shuffle and crop operations while maintaining style, we eliminated dependence on synthetic triplets and bypassed the need for explicit or implicit disentanglement modules. Our diffusion-based model achieves near-realistic fidelity and robust content accuracy, effectively narrowing the synthetic-to-real gap that limits previous STE approaches. Comprehensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that TextRIRO surpasses existing STE methods in both correctness and visual realism. Additionally, we create large-scale, realistic long-text recognition dataset, TextRIRO-3M. Training STR models on it yielded significant gains, proving that high-realism STE continues to propel STR performance beyond current saturation points. Naturally, TextRIRO excels in English thanks to abundant real scene text data, but such multilingual data is scarce. Future work will focus on accurate and realistic multilingual STE in low-resource settings.

6.3 Datasets and Implementation Details
Training Datasets. Our self-paired pipeline uses the text label and, in particular, its length, but it does
not require character segmentation. For Shuffle, we split the image width into nsplit ∈ 2, L equal-width
columns, where L is the label length, and randomly permute the columns. Crop takes a horizontal contiguous
sub-interval. Thus, a character may be cut by a column boundary. This is intentional because the purpose is
to remove readable semantics while retaining local visual style. We train our STE model and the STR baseline
on Union14M [16], currently the largest available scene text dataset. Specifically, we adopt a filtered version
of its labeled subset, denoted as U14M-Filter [7], which contains 3.22M annotated text instances. Note that
training in a completely label-free manner is theoretically infeasible, because the definition of STE inherently
requires specifying the edited text.
sections.content: Evaluation Datasets. To evaluate scene text editing performance under real-world conditions, we first employ the ScenePair [43], which comprises 1,280 pairs of carefully collected, real-world text images. Furthermore, we construct benchmarks for equal-length and variable-length text editing using six widely-used text recognition datasets: IIIT 5K-Words (IIIT [24]), ICDAR2013 (IC13 [17]), Street View Text (SVT [34]), ICDAR2015 (IC15 [18]), Street View Text-Perspective (SVTP [25]), and CUTE80 (CUTE [27]), which we collectively refer to as the Common Benchmarks. Additionally, we assess data quality using Union14M-Benchmark [16], which includes seven subsets: Curve (CUR), Multi-Oriented (MLO), Artistic (ART), Contextless (CTL), Salient (SAL), Multi-Words (MLW), and General (GEN). Implementation Details. We use MAERec [16] both for text-encoder pre-training and as our STR proxy baseline, training for 20 epochs under the settings established by the OpenOCR framework [7]. TextRIRO builds upon SD 2.1 for the VAE and SD 1.5 for the U-Net backbone [28]. The extensively pre-trained VAE in SD 2.1 is well-suited for scene text tasks. The U-Net requires its parameters to be unfrozen for training, so the specific version has minimal impact. Meanwhile, SD 1.5 uses smaller dimension (dim = 768) and can directly match the feature dimension of the text encoder. All images are resized to 64 256 and those with aspect ratios less than 1 : 2 are rotated 90 counterclockwise to match the target resolution. We use batch size of 256, apply an initial learning rate of 1 105, and train for 15 epochs on 8 NVIDIA V100 GPUs. During inference, we use 20 sampling steps and classifier-free guidance (CFG) scale of ω = 2.2. For the 15 generation of the TextRIRO-3M dataset, we use only reference images whose original text contains at least 4 characters. Consequently, the minimum label length in TextRIRO-3M is 8. For the other STE models, we use their officially reported results when available. Otherwise, we use their released official checkpoints and the default inference hyperparameters to ensure fair comparison. Traininginference protocol. During training, the style condition is the perturbed view of the same real image and the target text is its original label. At inference, the source is an unperturbed real image and the target is new string. This is an unavoidable residual mismatch because coherent real sourcetarget pairs with different text are not available at scale. Shuffle&Crop is designed to reduce the mismatch by producing real-image-derived style condition whose semantics are destroyed but whose local appearance remains realistic. The self-paired objective also provides content-disentanglement constraint: the source condition has disrupted text order, while the target text is supplied only through the text encoder. If semantic content leaked through the style path, the model would copy the disrupted content rather than render the correctly ordered target. Consistently, the identity (None) ablation in Fig. 4 collapses to an ACC of 4.37, showing that an unperturbed source encourages copying instead of text-conditioned editing. Computational Overhead and Runtime Efficiency. We report the computational requirements for both the STR pre-training and U-Net fine-tuning stages, which use 36 GPU-hours and 180 GPU-hours, respectively. For inference, we evaluate our method on single NVIDIA V100 GPU with diffusion_steps set to 20 and batch size of 32. Processing 10,000 batches requires 18 hours, corresponding to an average inference time of 0.20 seconds per image. 6.4 Additional Editing Evaluation
Per-image style fidelity beyond FID. FID is established as the evaluation metric in MOSTEL [26], and
TextCtrl [43] continues to use the same evaluation code to report FID on ScenePair, so we keep it for
comparability. For each generated image, we compare it against its corresponding ScenePair reference image
and report LPIPS (perceptual similarity), SSIM (structural similarity), and PSNR (pixel-level fidelity). Lower
LPIPS and higher SSIM and PSNR indicate better agreement with the paired reference. LPIPS measures
per-image perceptual and structural similarity, and FID measures how close the overall image distribution
is to the reference distribution. TextRIRO achieves the best results on both in Tab. 12, which indicates that
it generates images closer to the real distribution. PSNR and SSIM, in contrast, are per-image pixel-level
metrics that are sensitive to small spatial shifts, anti-aliasing, and valid appearance variations in rendered
text. Because the ScenePair reference images are manually collected and not strictly pixel-aligned pairs, even
a more realistic generation can score lower on these metrics simply because its pixels do not exactly match the
reference.

sections.title: 7.1 Character-Aware Embeddings
sections.content: The STR pre-trained text encoder endows TextRIRO with strong character awareness. To further evaluate its encoding capabilities, we visualize the embeddings of several text samples using t-SNE [23], as illustrated in Fig. 7. Overall, words with similar character compositions or comparable text lengths are positioned closer together, while sufficient separation is maintained between distinct samples. For example, the characters 1 and possess different semantic meanings but exhibit similar glyphs, resulting in 1024 and l024 being embedded in close proximity. Traditionally, glyph-pre-training is required for such nuanced feature representations, yet STR pre-training achieves this directly. Additionally, the variations there, There, THere, and THERE are embedded near each other, reflecting their shared underlying structure, yet each maintains distinct position. This separation prevents case confusion in text generation, thereby enabling accurate character-level generation.

sections.title: 7.4 Bad Cases and Discussion
sections.content: It is important to acknowledge that our STE approach is not without limitations. Fig. 11 illustrates three common failure cases, along with the corresponding causes and potential solutions: 1. Long Text: The text encoder used in our training pipeline is pre-trained from the STR model, which is primarily trained on datasets containing short text, resulting in limited capacity for capturing long text dependencies. Additionally, TextRIRO is trained on the same datasets, further constraining its ability to handle long text. To address this, we are inspired by the construction of the TextRIRO-3M dataset: we segment long text into shorter fragments, synthesize each fragment individually, and then concatenate these fragments to form the final long text. This approach leverages the inherent strengths of short text synthesis while enabling robust long text generation. 2. Curved Text and Complex Geometry: As shown in Fig. 11, TextRIRO recognizes that the input is not standard horizontally aligned text, but may interpret highly curved text as slanted. Crop preserves local tilt and curvature, and near-vertical inputs are rotated in preprocessing. Consequently, TextRIRO achieves equal-/variable-length accuracy of 64.87/48.12 on CUTE and 79.69/42.31 on SVTP, outperforming the compared baselines. Tab. 4 further isolates the operator contribution. However, extreme curvature and large geometric deformation remain difficult because regular layouts dominate the training data. Future work should incorporate finer-grained control points, similar to TPS modules in STR, to enable more precise geometric control. 3. Special Symbols and Languages: The synthesis of special symbols remains challenging because of both sparse training coverage and the current vocabulary/data coverage. This also restricts cross-lingual generalization: the self-pairing operation itself is language-agnostic, but sufficiently large real labeled datasets are currently much more available for Latin scripts than for low-resource languages. Collecting balanced real labeled data with broader character and language coverage is necessary for stable multilingual generation. TextRIRO will also provide more abundant synthetic data for multilingual and general OCR [8, 41]. 20 Figure 9 Length distributions of real data (U14M-Filter) and the original symmetric TextRIRO-3M construction. The symmetric recipe doubles the source length and hence produces even-length samples, and the asymmetric-augmented recipe in Tab. 13 removes this construction artifact. Shuffle preserves stroke thickness because it permutes equalwidth columns without rescaling them. Crop can change apparent stroke scale, but the two operators are complementary: pure-Shuffle instances remain in training with non-trivial probability (approximately 20% for an average label length of five) and anchor stroke-width preservation, while Crop supplies the scale variation needed for variable-length editing. The style encoder is not given an explicit transformation-type label, and it learns from the mixed perturbation distribution. Together with the disrupted semantics in the source and the separate text condition, this prevents simple content copying, as further supported by the None ablation described above. These mechanisms do not eliminate every failure case, but explain why the combined operator is more robust than either component alone.

sections.title: 8 Responsible Research Notes
sections.content: Broader impacts and safeguards. TextRIRO can support benign applications such as visual content localization, accessibility, and realistic STR data generation, but scene text editing can also be misused to falsify text in images. We therefore intend to release code, data-construction scripts, and TextRIRO-3M with clear research-use and acceptable-use notices, retain STR-based quality filtering, and encourage provenance tracking or watermarking when the technology is deployed. Existing assets and licenses. The work uses publicly available academic datasets, model components, and baselines, all cited in the main paper and bibliography. Users of released artifacts will be instructed to follow the original licenses and terms for Union14M, U14M-Filter, ScenePair, the STR benchmarks, Stable Diffusion components, and compared open-source STE models. The instruction was: Given generated image and its target label, mark the sample correct only if all visible characters match the target label in order.
